extracted.intended_audience: EPA and state regulators; electric utilities, cooperatives, pipeline companies, and regulatory/legal counsel preparing comments on EPA Section 111(d) proposal
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing formal regulatory comments assessing the legality, feasibility, and reliability impacts of EPA's proposed Section 111(d) greenhouse gas rule (the Proposed Rule), with emphasis on Building Blocks 2 and 3 (natural gas dispatch and nuclear/renewables).

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC preemption and pipeline authorization constraints (impact on Building Block 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC regulation preempts many of the actions Building Block 2 assumes the States will take. Unlike new electric transmission, new interstate natural gas transmission facilities must receive FERC review and authorization. FERC generally does not authorize new pipeline capacity unless customers have already committed to using it (i.e., have firm delivery contracts), and pipelines are prohibited from charging the cost of new capacity to their existing customer base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because FERC approves new facilities only after new customers have requested firm service, there will be little or no excess pipeline capacity to support NGCC units’ efforts to achieve the 70% capacity factor target unless developers secure firm customers first. This regulatory structure undermines EPA's assumption that additional pipeline capacity will be available to support re-dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting and stakeholder delays for pipeline construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A host of federal, state, regional, and local approvals are necessary for pipeline construction to begin. Urban encroachment on rights-of-way, multi-stakeholder opposition (landowners, environmentalists), and numerous statutory approvals (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, ESA, etc.) can impede projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines vary: less controversial/smaller projects can be built within a year if permits are timely; large projects may take a decade or decades (e.g., Alaska pipeline). EPA's suggested phase-in cannot reliably address or predict these permitting and siting delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependencies between natural gas and electric industries must be accounted for
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule fails to account for the complex interdependencies between the natural gas and electricity industries. Gas-fired generators relying on congested pipelines face frequent supply issues; when plants cannot receive fuel to operate in response to ISO/RTO dispatch, reliability is threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing work at FERC and standards organizations may improve coordination, but progress is uncertain; EPA cannot assume these interdependencies will be resolved in time to meet compliance timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational constraints demonstrated during extreme events (Polar Vortex examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the 2013-2014 Polar Vortex pipelines imposed Hourly-Takes Advisories, Operational Flow Orders, and Critical Time Declarations that limited generators' flexibility, imposed penalties, and restricted access to storage. Examples: AECC limited for 66 days; Wolverine couldn't access storage despite having gas; Hoosier Energy ran only 4 days (capacity factor 1%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These real-world operational constraints show that even with pipeline contracts or storage, gas-fired generators may be unable to respond to dispatch, undermining EPA's reliance on NGCC re-dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipelines inherently limited in flexibility for non-ratable, variable electric loads
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipelines were initially designed for steady hourly load profiles (1/24 of daily consumption each hour). Daily and weekly variations and non-ratable takes from electric loads are particularly difficult for pipelines to accommodate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pipelines are unlikely to provide necessary fuel for daily peak electricity demand; reliance on pipelines for variable electric loads overestimates pipeline operational capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: High pressure requirements of modern gas-fired generators strain pipeline operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Newer, larger combustion turbine/combined cycle units require consistent and often higher fuel pressures and are less tolerant of pressure variations than older units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher pressure requirements reduce pipeline flexibility and response capability, a constraint EPA does not sufficiently recognize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic mismatch of gas supply and rural cooperative loads
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas suppliers and pipelines are significantly limited or absent in many rural areas where electric cooperative baseload facilities are located; pipelines may be hundreds of miles away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where pipelines exist, availability of firm gas supplies at reasonable price is uncertain; EPA's uniform assumptions ignore regional/geographic disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for anchor customers and contract uncertainty for new pipeline development
rubrics_metrics.description: Gas pipeline developers are reluctant to build without 'anchor' customers and firm long-term contracts; generation owners will not commit without certainty about long-term dispatch under EPA's rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This circular uncertainty — pipelines need firm customers, customers need dispatch certainty, EPA creates dispatch uncertainty — undermines the feasibility of Building Block 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits on BSER: EPA cannot require new generation or fuel switching as BSER for existing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: It is blatantly unlawful for EPA to require the construction of new generation assets or require co-firing as part of BSER for existing sources. Requiring co-firing is tantamount to fuel switching, which EPA has stated is not BSER. BSER must reduce emissions within the source category and be applied at the affected facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BSER cannot lawfully be applied outside the specified source category (fossil fuel-fired EGUs); EPA's inclusion of Building Block 3 (nuclear and renewables) and requirement of new NGCC construction/co-firing as BSER is legally unsupportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA lacks authority to set regional generation/emission targets under Section 111(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in Section 111(d) gives EPA authority to set regional generation or emission targets. Section 111(d) provides for state-specific standards of performance and reserves to individual States the authority to set those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying targeted levels of generation shift for multi-state regions would be unlawful and undermine state primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission expansion timelines and planning processes are long and complex
rubrics_metrics.description: After EPA accepts state plans, it will take ~2+ years for generation/transmission entities to analyze potential system requirements; then regional planning typically takes an additional ~2 years. In best circumstances, 4–5 years are necessary before an approved transmission plan can be achieved; some projects take 10+ years or never get built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's targets and timelines do not accommodate planning, permitting, siting, rights-of-way acquisition, cost allocation negotiations, and public opposition inherent in transmission build-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting, rights-of-way, endangered species and other environmental reviews add uncertainty and delay to transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits for endangered species, historic preservation, water quality, tribal rights-of-way, and other federal/state approvals are 'moving targets' and can add substantial delay and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must account for evolving listings (e.g., USFWS candidate species) and multi-jurisdictional permitting complexity when assuming transmission can be expanded promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: High and variable transmission construction costs affect feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical costs vary substantially by voltage and whether overhead or underground: e.g., new 69 kV overhead ~$285,000/mile vs underground ~$1.5M/mile; overhead 138 kV ~$390,000/mile vs underground ~$2M/mile; urban/suburban/rural ranges up to millions per mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entities are unlikely to risk expensive transmission expansion if the electricity is expected to be displaced soon; EPA underestimates cost barriers and investment risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building Block 3 (nuclear and renewables) cannot be part of BSER for legal reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Nuclear and renewable generation do not fall within the target source category and cannot be BSER. BSER must reduce emissions within a source category at affected facilities. Replacing generation with zero-emitting generation outside the source category is not BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's inclusion of Building Block 3 in BSER is asserted to be 'plainly unlawful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's assumptions on renewable growth and regional averaging are unsupported and arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assumes non-hydro renewable generation will increase dramatically (217,868 GWh in 2012 to 522,723 GWh in 2029) and applies regional growth factors and un-weighted averages of state RPS goals, excluding states without RPSs from averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's methodology ignores state-specific factors (costs, transmission availability, economic development priorities, RPS design features like cost caps/waivers) and treats regions as homogenous, which is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper use and interpretation of state RPS statutes in setting targets
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA extracted numeric standards from some RPSs (e.g., Kansas, North Carolina) without applying other statutory determinants (capacity vs energy basis, applicability only to certain utilities, inclusion of hydro or other resources, cost caps, waiver provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misreading RPS statutes produces unrealistic regional targets (e.g., Arkansas target should reflect Kansas capacity-based RPS converted to energy basis), so EPA's targets are unsupportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to address cost allocation for additional renewables and transmission undermines meaningful comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal fails to explain how costs of renewable resources and needed transmission will be allocated and who has responsibility to mandate allocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a proposed cost-allocation mechanism, stakeholders cannot meaningfully comment on distributional impacts and market risk; political and legal dynamics of cost allocation are material to feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary treatment of interstate renewable generation (only in-state counted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike state RPSs and actual market behavior, the proposal's goals only recognize renewable resources developed within state borders and ignore power transmitted interstate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because electric systems are integrated and benefits/capacity cross state lines, excluding interstate renewable development is arbitrary and misstates practical resource deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for intermediate/flexible backup generation and system balancing for variable renewables
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant portion of additional renewables (especially wind) is intermittent and will require reliable backup generation to ensure grid reliability and maintain frequency/voltage tolerances. CAISO reports insufficient flexible generator capacity to accommodate increasing wind/solar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA fails to consider capital and O&M costs for increased flexible capacity, transmission build-outs, and integration services; these costs will be borne by ratepayers and are not accounted for in EPA's analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most renewable generation developers are not regulated entities under the proposal; States lack authority to force renewables without legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: The entities building renewable generation (e.g., wind developers) are not in the identified source category and thus are not affected entities under the proposal. Most States cannot mandate additional renewables through regulators alone—state legislatures must enact authority, which can take years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's reliance on States mandating additional renewables ignores the political and legal limits on state authority and the long legislative timelines, making the proposal's assumptions about renewables deployment unrealistic.
